etymology: Old English heardian, from heard (hard). Renders the Hebrew qāshāh, “to be hard, stiff,” chāzaq, “to make strong, harden,” and kābad (hiphil), “to make heavy”; and the Greek sklērunō, “to harden,” and pōroō, “to petrify, render insensible.”
biblical_def: To harden, in Scripture, is to render a heart unresponsive, callous, or insensible to God’s Word, Spirit, and providence—and the verb is used both of God’s judicial hardening of the rebel and of the rebel’s own self-hardening against grace. The Pharaoh narrative of Exodus is the textbook case: Pharaoh hardens his own heart (Ex 8:15, 32; 9:34), and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart (Ex 9:12; 10:1, 20; 11:10); the two stand together without contradiction, and Paul appeals to the same case in Romans 9 to set forth God’s sovereignty over the hard heart: therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. The biblical anatomy of hardening is sober. It is rarely a sudden act and almost always a process: the conscience repeatedly resists known truth, the affections cool toward God, the will refuses to yield, and the heart over time grows callous to what once pricked it. Hebrews 3–4 sets the warning at its most pastoral pitch: today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness; the writer charges his hearers to exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. The hardening is the soul’s loss of softness to the Spirit’s touch—a deafening of the inward ear, a calcification of the inward eye, an unresponsive heart where there was once a tender one. Its end is the awful judicial reprobation in which God hands the hardened soul over to its chosen darkness: Romans 1 thrice repeats God gave them up. Its remedy is repentance under the Word and the breaking of the soul before the cross, where God promises to take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and give you an heart of flesh. To hear of hardening and to feel any softening at the warning is itself a token of grace; to hear and be unmoved is the very symptom the warning addresses.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HARDEN as to make hard or harder; to confirm in effrontery, in wickedness, or in obstinacy; to render insensible or unfeeling.
webster_full: HARDEN, v.t. — 1. To make hard or more hard; to make firm or compact. 2. To confirm in effrontery; to make impudent. 3. To confirm in wickedness, obstinacy, or any evil course; as, to harden the heart. 4. To render insensible or unfeeling; as, to harden the conscience.
HARDENING, ppr. — Making hard or more hard; making obdurate, unfeeling, or obstinate; confirming in effrontery or in wickedness.
scriptures: Hebrews 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Hebrews 3:15
While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.
Exodus 9:12
And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had spoken unto Moses.
Romans 9:18
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of hardening is corrupted by the therapeutic age’s denial that there is such a thing as a calloused soul—every soul is treated as soft, tender, and merely needing more affirmation—and by the inverse error that treats hardening as so total and judicial that it removes responsibility from the one whose own daily resistance to God’s Word produced it.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic age cannot recognize hardening because it does not believe in the moral diagnosis on which hardening rests. Where Scripture says the resisted Word, the indulged sin, and the rejected Spirit produce a calloused heart, the therapeutic register insists that all hearts remain tender beneath the surface and that the appearance of hardness is only unmet need. The result is pastoral malpractice. The hardened are told they are wounded; the calloused conscience is treated as a tender one; the warning passages of Hebrews 3–4 are read as encouragement and never as the sober rebuke they are; and the very softness the warning aims to recover is forfeited because the diagnosis the warning depends on has been denied. Recover the biblical diagnosis, and the warnings recover their force: today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.

The opposite corruption removes responsibility by treating hardening as a fixed judicial act in which the person became merely a passive object of God’s reprobating decree. The Pharaoh narrative refuses both errors. Pharaoh hardens his own heart and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart; the two stand together throughout the chapters; the self-hardening is real and culpable, and the divine hardening is real and sovereign. The pastoral application follows: every act of resisting known truth, of indulging known sin, of refusing the Spirit’s touch, contributes to the soul’s present softness or hardness; and the sober use of the warning is to keep today in view—to soften under the Word in this hour, before the deceitfulness of sin works the calcification it always works when given time.
roots_summary: Hebrew qāshāh (to be hard), chāzaq (to make strong), kābad (hiphil—to make heavy); Greek sklērunō (to harden) and pōroō (to petrify, render insensible)—the calcification of the heart against God’s Word, Spirit, and providence.

Hebrew chāzaq (H2388) — to be strong, to harden (used of Pharaoh’s heart).
Greek sklērunō (G4645) — to harden (Heb 3:8, 13, 15; Acts 19:9; Rom 9:18).

usage: Hardening is rarely sudden and almost always a process—the conscience that repeatedly resists known truth becomes the conscience that no longer feels the touch.
Pharaoh hardens his own heart and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart—both true, both stated in the same chapters, and both refused by the therapeutic and the fatalistic corruptions alike.
Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts—the warning’s force is preserved only where the diagnosis it depends on is preserved.

etymology: Latin humilis (lowly, on the ground), from humus (earth). Renders the Hebrew ‘ānāh, “to afflict, humble,” and shāphēl, “to be low”; and the Greek tapeinoō, “to make low, humble.”
biblical_def: To humble (as a verb) is the active making-low of the proud soul—either by God’s providential dealings or by the saint’s own deliberate act of self-humbling under the mighty hand of God. The Bible uses the verb in both directions, and the two are inseparable. God humbles: He humbled Pharaoh, He humbled Nebuchadnezzar at the height of his pride until he ate grass like the oxen, He humbles every soul who exalts itself against Him—for God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble, and he that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted. The saint humbles himself: James and Peter both press the same command—humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up; humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The pattern of biblical humbling is therefore active and willed, not merely the slumped posture of a beaten man. The saint takes the lower seat at the feast, lest he be told to give place; he confesses his sin instead of excusing it; he yields to authority where authority is owed; he refuses the inward boast and the outward display; he reckons others better than himself, esteems them more highly; he washes feet because his Master washed feet, and he counts no service beneath him because the Son of God counted no service beneath Him. The supreme model is Christ: he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; and the supreme law is the inversion that runs through the kingdom: the way up is down, the great is the servant, the first is the last, and the humbled soul is the exalted one. Apart from active humbling, all subsequent graces wither; with it, the soul stands in the very place where God delights to give grace.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HUMBLE as to abase; to reduce to a low state; to crush; to subdue; to make submissive; in religion, to repress what is haughty in oneself and to walk softly before God.
webster_full: HUMBLE, v.t. — 1. To abase; to reduce to a low state. 2. To crush; to subdue; to break, as the spirit or pride. 3. To make submissive; as, to humble an enemy. 4. In religion, to repress what is haughty in oneself; to lower oneself in one’s own estimation, and to walk softly before God.
HUMBLING, ppr. — Abasing; reducing to a low condition or rank; subduing pride; rendering submissive or modest.
scriptures: James 4:10
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.
1 Peter 5:6
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.
Philippians 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Micah 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: The verb humble is corrupted by the false humility of the age—the curated self-deprecation that performs lowliness while jealously guarding the inward boast—and by the inverse pride of the assertiveness culture that despises self-humbling as weakness and refuses the inversion at the heart of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has two characteristic corruptions of humbling, and the believer absorbs both. The first is performed false humility: the carefully curated self-deprecation, the visible token of lowliness offered up for social credit, the boast disguised as confession (‘my biggest weakness is that I work too hard’)—the form of humility without the substance, retaining the inward pride while presenting the outward posture. Scripture is sharper than this: the humbling commanded is not a performance for human view but a real lowering of the soul before God, who sees through every performance and resists the proud even when the proud have learned to perform humility well. The cure is not better performance but the actual act of self-humbling—confessing what is actually true, taking the lower seat in reality, esteeming others better in fact, refusing the inward boast that the performance was meant to mask.

The opposite and more contemporary corruption is the assertiveness culture’s active despising of self-humbling as weakness. The believer is told from every corner of the surrounding world to assert himself, to lean in, to know his worth, to never apologize, to refuse to be made small—and the gospel-shaped inversion that says he that humbleth himself shall be exalted is felt as a relic of a backward and crushing era. But the inversion is not optional Christianity; it is the inner shape of the kingdom and the imitation of the King who humbled Himself to the death of the cross. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers both the freedom and the dignity of the lower seat: the freedom from the exhausting labor of self-promotion, and the dignity of walking the road his Master walked—the road that ends not in obscurity but in exaltation, in due time, by the very hand under which the soul learned to be humbled.
roots_summary: Hebrew ‘ānāh (to afflict, humble) and shāphēl (to be low); Greek tapeinoō (to make low, humble)—both God’s providential humbling and the saint’s active self-humbling under His mighty hand.
roots_lines: Hebrew ‘ānāh (H6031) — to afflict, humble, oppress; both God’s humbling of His people and the soul’s self-affliction.
Hebrew shāphēl (H8213) — to be low, abased, brought down.
Greek tapeinoō (G5013) — to make low, humble (James 4:10; 1 Pet 5:6; Phil 2:8).
Greek tapeinophrosunē (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility (the noun).

He humbled himself—the supreme model is Christ, who set aside the use of His prerogatives and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Curated self-deprecation and assertiveness culture corrupt the verb in opposite directions; biblical humbling is the real lowering of the soul before God who sees through both.

etymology: Old English hungrian, from hungor (hunger). Renders the Hebrew rā‘ēb, “to be hungry,” and the Greek peinaō, “to hunger, be hungry,” used both of bodily hunger and of the soul’s longing for God and His righteousness.
biblical_def: To hunger, in Scripture, is to feel the urgent inward emptiness that craves to be filled—most literally of the body’s need for food, but transferred by the Spirit’s use to the soul’s deep need for God Himself, His Word, and His righteousness. The Beatitude is the verb’s charter: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. The blessedness lies precisely in the hunger; the unhungry soul is not commended; the satisfied-with-self soul receives nothing because it craves nothing. Christ in the wilderness, after forty days, was an hungered—and met the tempter with the deeper word: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. The saint’s hunger is therefore a moral and spiritual organ. He hungers after Christ as the bread of life; he hungers for the Word as the necessary daily food; he hungers for righteousness as the famished man hungers for bread, with the energy of need; he hungers for the day when his Lord shall return and he shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, for the Lamb shall feed him and lead him to living fountains of waters. The biblical contrast is sharp: the Laodicean church says I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and Christ counsels her to buy of Him gold tried in the fire—the rebuke is that she has lost hunger. The Spirit’s ordinary work in awakening a soul is the awakening of holy hunger; the absence of hunger is the most ominous spiritual symptom; the presence of even small hunger is the most hopeful spiritual sign, because the promise stands: they shall be filled.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HUNGER as an uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food; a craving of food by the stomach; figuratively, any strong or eager desire.
webster_full: HUNGER, v.i. — 1. To feel the pain or uneasiness which is occasioned by long abstinence from food. 2. To desire with great eagerness; to long for. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness (Matt 5:6).
HUNGER, n. — 1. An uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food. 2. Any strong or eager desire.
scriptures: Matthew 5:6
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
Matthew 4:4
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
John 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Revelation 7:16-17
They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more... For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters.
corruption_summary: Spiritual hungering is corrupted by the over-fed satiety of late-modern consumer culture, which has trained the soul to be perpetually filled with lesser things and never to feel the holy emptiness that the gospel addresses—and by the Laodicean self-sufficiency that says I have need of nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Late-modern consumer culture is a discipline in the elimination of hunger. The body is perpetually fed and snacked between meals; the eye is perpetually fed with screens; the ear is perpetually fed with audio; the affections are perpetually fed with entertainment; the appetites are catered to faster than they can form into hunger. The result is a generation whose soul, like its body, has never been allowed to be empty, and which therefore has lost the capacity to feel the deep hunger after God to which the Beatitude promises filling. The believer absorbs the discipline of satiety and brings it to prayer, worship, and the Word with the same dulled appetite he brings to everything else: a soul too well-fed by lesser things to hunger for the better. Recover hunger by removing some of the lesser feedings—the fast, the screen-off, the deliberate spiritual hunger-pang—and the deeper appetites return.

The Laodicean corruption is hunger’s self-flattering twin: the soul that says I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and does not realize that it is wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. The most dangerous spiritual state is not the felt emptiness that drives a soul to Christ but the felt fullness that keeps a soul away. The Beatitude reverses the world’s ranking: blessed are not the satisfied but the hungry, not the filled but the empty, not the rich-in-self but the poor-in-spirit. Where the felt-sufficient cannot be helped, the hungry shall be filled. The recovery is therefore both a discipline (fast from the lesser fillings) and a confession (own the actual emptiness), and the promise stands at the end of both: they shall be filled.
roots_summary: Hebrew rā‘ēb (to be hungry) and Greek peinaō (to hunger)—both bodily hunger and the soul’s deep craving for God, the Word, the bread of life, and the righteousness that the Beatitude promises shall be filled.
roots_lines: Hebrew rā‘ēb (H7456) — to be hungry, to suffer hunger.
Greek peinaō (G3983) — to hunger, be hungry; used in the Beatitude and of Christ’s wilderness hunger.
Hebrew rā‘āb (H7458) — hunger, famine (the noun).
Greek limos (G3042) — famine, severe hunger.
usage: Blessedness lies precisely in the hunger—the unhungry soul is not commended; the satisfied-with-self soul receives nothing because it craves nothing.
The Laodicean state (I have need of nothing) is the most dangerous spiritual condition; the hunger-recovered state is the most hopeful.
Late-modern consumer culture is a discipline in the elimination of hunger; the cure is the discipline of fasting from the lesser feedings to recover the deeper appetite.

etymology: Old English þyrstan, from þurst (thirst). Renders the Hebrew tsāmē’, “to thirst,” and the Greek dipsaō, “to thirst, be thirsty,” used both of the body’s craving for water and of the soul’s deep longing for God, righteousness, and the living water of Christ.
biblical_def: To thirst is to feel the urgent inward dryness that craves to be slaked—at its first reference the body’s need for water, at its deepest the soul’s need for God Himself. The Psalms set the verb’s great register: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God? And again: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is. Christ at the Feast of Tabernacles stood and cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water; and the apostle adds, this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive. The promise is universal: whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; the gospel offer is universal: and the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely; and the consummation is universal: I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely. Thirst is therefore the saint’s blessed inward register: the longing that drives him to the Fountain, the dryness that craves the springs of living water, the panting after God which is itself the Spirit’s evidence that the soul has been awakened. Christ Himself thirsted on the cross—a bodily thirst and, beneath it, the deeper drying-up of the soul under the wrath that bought us the living water we now drink. Thirst recovered is the soul recovered; thirst maintained is the soul healthy; thirst quenched, in the consummation, is the soul at last home: they shall thirst no more, neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat. For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THIRST as a painful sensation occasioned by the want of drink; figuratively, a vehement desire of anything; an eager longing.
webster_full: THIRST, v.i. — 1. To feel a painful sensation of the throat or fauces for want of drink; to feel a desire for drink. 2. To have a vehement desire of any thing. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God (Psa 42:2).
THIRST, n. — 1. The sensation occasioned by the want of drink; eagerness for drink. 2. A vehement desire of anything; as, a thirst for praise, for fame, for knowledge.
scriptures: Psalm 42:1-2
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.
Matthew 5:6
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
...If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
Revelation 22:17
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: Spiritual thirsting is corrupted by the over-irrigated soul of the contemporary believer, who quenches every inward dryness with lesser drinks (entertainment, social media, busyness, the addictive comforts) and never lets the deep thirst form—and by the Jeremianic broken-cistern corruption of preferring the cisterns we hew out for ourselves to the fountain of living waters.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary believer is rarely permitted to be spiritually thirsty. Every inward dryness, every felt emptiness, every quiet ache of the soul is met immediately by the nearest lesser drink: the scroll of the phone, the next show, the snack, the conversation that fills the silence, the busyness that fills the calendar. The very dryness that, if allowed to form, would drive the soul to the springs of living waters is quenched in advance by an over-irrigated life of small consolations. The result is a generation that knows it is not satisfied but cannot articulate the thirst, because every formation of thirst is interrupted before it reaches its proper depth. The cure is the willingness to be dry—to turn off the lesser fountains, to let the silence and emptiness form, to permit the soul to discover its actual thirst, and to bring that thirst to the Fountain who alone can slake it.

The Jeremianic indictment is the older and graver corruption: my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water. Two evils, the LORD names. The first is forsaking the Fountain; the second is the active labor of digging cisterns of our own—careers, comforts, achievements, idols of every shape—to hold what they can never hold. The cisterns leak; the labor is endless; the thirst persists; and the Fountain stands forsaken. The recovery is the double turn the gospel announces and the soul, by the Spirit, performs: away from the broken cisterns, back to the Fountain. If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink—the offer is wide enough for every weary digger of broken cisterns and tender enough for every secret thirst no other water has slaked.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsāmē’ (to thirst) and Greek dipsaō (to thirst)—the soul’s deep longing for God set against the broken cisterns of Jeremiah 2 and answered by the living water of John 4 and 7.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsāmē’ (H6770) — to thirst, to be thirsty.
Hebrew tsāmā’ (H6772) — thirst (the noun).
Greek dipsaō (G1372) — to thirst (Matt 5:6; John 4:13-15; 7:37; 19:28; Rev 21:6; 22:17).
Greek dipsos (G1373) — thirst (the noun, 2 Cor 11:27).

The over-irrigated soul of the contemporary believer never permits the deep thirst to form; recovery requires the willingness to be dry long enough for the proper craving to surface.
Two evils, says Jeremiah: forsaking the Fountain, and digging our own broken cisterns—the Fountain still stands, the offer is still wide, if any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.

etymology: Old Norse kasta, “to throw, hurl.” Renders many Hebrew and Greek verbs of throwing, casting down, casting out, and casting upon; principally the Greek ballō, “to throw,” ekballō, “to cast out,” and epirhiptō, “to cast upon” (1 Pet 5:7).
biblical_def: Cast, in the King James Bible, is one of the most freighted verbs in Scripture, carrying a dozen distinct biblical actions according to its preposition and object. To cast out is the verb of exorcism: Christ casts out devils with a word, the disciples are given authority to cast them out, the demons depart at His command. To cast down is to bring low: casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God—the believer’s offensive weapon against speculative pride. To cast off is the act of God in repudiation: Israel feared the LORD had cast them off forever, and Romans 11 returns the question, hath God cast away his people? God forbid. To cast lots is to seek the divine arbitration of an uncertain matter: the apostles cast lots for Judas’s replacement; the disposing of the lot is wholly of the LORD. To cast away is to forfeit: cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward. To cast in one’s lot with another is to throw in one’s portion with theirs (Prov 1:14). And, supremely for the believer’s daily life, to cast upon is the verb of 1 Peter 5:7: casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. The picture is decisive and active: a deliberate throwing of one’s burdens onto Another, not a vague hope that He notices them. The casting is the disposition of the heart in prayer: every anxiety identified, named, and thrown by an act of the will onto the broad shoulders of the Father who has shown He can bear them. The same verb gathers up the great eschatological actions of God: the devil cast into the lake of fire, death and hell cast into the lake of fire, every name not written in the book of life cast in with them. Cast is therefore one of the Bible’s decisive verbs: it does not negotiate, drift, or wish; it throws.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CAST as to throw, fling, or send; to throw down or to throw with violence; to direct or turn, as the eye; to throw out or eject, as from a place.
webster_full: CAST, v.t. — 1. To throw, fling, or send; that is, to drive from, by force, as from the hand, or from an engine. Cast thy bread upon the waters (Eccl 11:1). 2. To throw down or to throw with violence. 3. To direct or turn, as the eye; to throw the sight. 4. To throw out or eject, as from a place. 5. To deposit, as a vote. 6. To compute; to reckon, as accounts. 7. In scripture, to lay aside, as a hindrance; to throw upon another, as a burden; to throw away, as worthless.
CASTING, ppr. — Throwing; flinging; sending; computing; turning; rejecting; ejecting; casting upon.
scriptures: 1 Peter 5:7
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
2 Corinthians 10:5
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.
Romans 11:1-2
I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid... God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.
Hebrews 10:35
Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward.
corruption_summary: The believer’s biblical casting is corrupted by the chronic-anxiety register of the age, in which the burden is endlessly carried in the hand and never thrown by the soul onto the Father—and by the half-cast that briefly throws and then takes back, restoring the worry to the hand at the next provocation.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Peter 5:7 is one of Scripture’s most commonly misread verses. Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you is not an encouragement to be less anxious in the abstract; it is the command to perform a deliberate, willed action: a casting—an actual throwing—of the burden, by name and in detail, onto the Father who has invited the throw. The chronic-anxiety register of the contemporary believer collapses the verse into vague reassurance and never performs the casting. The burden remains in the hand. The worry persists, even while the verse is quoted. The cure is the act itself: the deliberate prayer, often spoken aloud, often listed by name, in which the anxieties are identified, surrendered, and committed, with the express purpose of leaving them with God and not picking them back up. The verse does not say be casting; it commands a casting that has a definite shape and a definite end.

The companion corruption is the half-cast, in which the soul throws the burden in prayer in the morning and takes it back at the first provocation in the afternoon. The pattern repeats: cast at devotions, retrieve at frustration, cast again at bedtime, retrieve at the next worried thought. The discipline of casting includes the discipline of refusing to retrieve. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. The peace is given not to the soul that casts and re-casts the same burden hourly, but to the soul that casts and then lets the peace of God do its garrisoning work. The verb cast is decisive; the saint’s practice of it must be decisive too.
roots_summary: Greek ballō (to throw), ekballō (to cast out), epirhiptō (to cast upon—1 Pet 5:7); Hebrew shālak (to throw, cast) and yārah (to throw, shoot)—a decisive throwing of burdens onto God, devils out of the soul, and high imaginations down to captivity.
roots_lines: Greek ballō (G906) — to throw, cast (the base verb).
Greek ekballō (G1544) — to cast out (exorcism, expulsion).
Greek epirhiptō (G1977) — to cast upon (1 Pet 5:7, “casting all your care upon him”).
Hebrew shālak (H7993) — to throw, cast, fling.
usage: Cast is a decisive verb—it does not negotiate, drift, or wish; it throws.
Casting one’s care is a willed action, not vague reassurance: a deliberate throwing of the burden by name onto the Father who has invited the throw.
Casting down imaginations is the believer’s offensive weapon against speculative pride—every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God.

etymology: Old Norse lypta, “to raise.” Renders the Hebrew nāsā’, “to lift, carry, bear,” and rūm, “to be high, exalted”; and the Greek epairō, “to lift up,” hupsoō, “to exalt,” and airo, “to take up, lift.”
biblical_def: Lift in Scripture is the verb of upward motion in worship, intercession, blessing, and divine help. The saint lifts up his hands in prayer (let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in the heavens); he lifts up his voice in praise and supplication; he lifts up his eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh his help; he lifts up the head of the bowed-down in Christ-shaped consolation; he lifts up holy hands without wrath and doubting; he lifts the fallen to their feet. God lifts: He is the lifter up of mine head; He lifteth up the meek; He lifteth up the poor out of the dust, and the needy from the dunghill; He lifts up His countenance upon His people in the Aaronic blessing. Christ lifts: He lifted up His eyes to the Father at Lazarus’s tomb and in the high-priestly prayer; He lifted up His hands and blessed the disciples as He was parted from them and carried up into heaven. And, supremely, Christ Himself is lifted up—on the cross (as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up), at His resurrection, at His ascension, and at the Father’s right hand. The verb’s grammar is therefore the gospel grammar: the lifted Christ lifts His people from death to life, from the dust to the heavenly places, from the bowed-down posture of guilt to the upright posture of sons. To lift up the hands, the voice, the eyes, the head, and the heart is the embodied liturgy of the saved—the bodily echo of the inward exaltation of the soul that has been lifted by grace and now lives in the upward motion that grace produces.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LIFT as to raise; to elevate; to bear or carry upward; figuratively, to raise to dignity, honor, or office; to exalt.
webster_full: LIFT, v.t. — 1. To raise; to elevate; as, to lift the hand, the head, the foot. 2. To raise from anything depressing; as, to lift up the head, the heart. 3. To raise in dignity, condition, or rank; to elevate; as, to lift to office. 4. In scripture, to elate; to make haughty; as, his heart was lifted up.
LIFTING, ppr. — Raising; bearing up; elevating; exalting.
scriptures: Psalm 121:1-2
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
1 Timothy 2:8
I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting.
John 3:14
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.
And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.
corruption_summary: The biblical lifting of hands, eyes, voice, and head is corrupted by the embarrassment of the rationalist evangelical register that has stiffened the body in worship into hands-in-pockets passivity—and by the inverse extreme of stage-managed performance lifting in charismatic spectacle that empties the gesture of its biblical content.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of the rationalist evangelical register has stiffened the body in worship into a posture of hands-in-pockets passivity that the Bible does not know. Scripture is unabashed about the body in worship: lifted hands (Ps 28:2; 63:4; 134:2; 1 Tim 2:8), lifted eyes (Ps 121:1; 123:1; Luke 24:50), lifted voice (Acts 4:24), bowed heads and bent knees in confession, prostrate bodies in awe—the soul’s adoration finding embodied expression because man is body-and-soul together and worships as he is. The cultural memory of revivalist emotionalism has produced, in much of the Reformed and quietly evangelical world, an over-correction in which any bodily lifting is read as suspicious enthusiasm and the believer is implicitly instructed to keep his hands at his sides. The text is sharper than this. I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting is not an optional posture for the temperamentally exuberant; it is the apostolic instruction for the body in prayer.

The opposite corruption is the stage-managed performance lifting of certain charismatic spectacle, in which the gesture has become disconnected from its biblical content and functions chiefly as a marker of in-group emotional intensity. The hands go up because the music swells, not because the soul has been moved to adore; the bodily form has become its own reference. Recover the biblical content, and the lifting recovers its meaning. The hands go up because the heart has gone up; the eyes go up because the help comes from above; the voice goes up because the soul has been given something to declare; the head goes up because the Father has lifted what guilt and sorrow had bowed. Both the over-stiffened and the over-performed traditions can find their cure in the same place: in recovering the Bible’s own grammar of lifting, which is the embodied liturgy of a people whose Lord has been lifted up, and who live forever after in the upward motion that grace produces.
roots_summary: Hebrew nāsā’ (to lift, carry, bear) and rūm (to be high); Greek epairō (to lift up), hupsoō (to exalt), and airo (to take up)—the upward verb of worship, intercession, blessing, and the lifted Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew nāsā’ (H5375) — to lift, carry, bear (the great verb behind “lift up” in the Psalms).
Hebrew rūm (H7311) — to be high, exalted, lifted up.
Greek epairō (G1869) — to lift up (eyes, hands, voice, the head).
Greek hupsoō (G5312) — to exalt, lift up (used of Christ’s being lifted up on the cross in John 3:14; 12:32).
usage: The lifted Christ lifts His people; the embodied liturgy of lifted hands, eyes, voice, and head is the bodily echo of the inward exaltation grace produces.
Hands-in-pockets passivity is not biblical reverence; it is the cultural over-correction of a tradition that has forgotten the apostolic instruction to lift holy hands.
As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up—all the lesser liftings in Scripture echo the supreme lifting at the cross.

etymology: Old English clingan, “to shrink, wither, hold fast.” Renders the Hebrew dābaq, “to stick, cling, cleave,” in its devotional-adhesion uses, and the Greek kollaō, “to join, glue, stick to.”
biblical_def: To cling, in Scripture, is the devotional adhesion of the soul to the LORD—the act by which the saint, having tasted that the LORD is good, refuses to let Him go and binds himself to Him with the whole weight of his trust, love, and life. The Hebrew dābaq is the great clinging verb of the Old Testament. It is used of the husband cleaving to his wife (Gen 2:24); it is the verb of Ruth’s loyalty to Naomi (and Ruth clave unto her); but its supreme use is devotional: that thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days (Deut 30:20); my soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me (Ps 63:8—the verb is dābaq, ‘to cling’); but ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day (Deut 4:4). The Greek kollaō carries the same picture into the New Testament: cleave to that which is good (Rom 12:9); and the verb stands behind the warning that he which is joined to an harlot is one body (1 Cor 6:16) and the promise that he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor 6:17). The clinging is therefore covenantal, exclusive, and total: the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty, and presses against the LORD as the only object worthy of so weighted a bond. The picture is bodily: the child who will not be pried from the parent, the bride who holds fast to the bridegroom, the climber whose whole weight is on the rope. Clinging is the saint’s posture in temptation (when nothing but the LORD will hold), in suffering (when the LORD is the only stable ground), in prosperity (when the soul that does not cling to Him will cling to His gifts and lose Him), and in death (when the clinging soul is met by the right hand that upholds and is brought safe through the valley to the everlasting hills).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CLING as to adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast upon, especially by winding round or embracing; figuratively, to adhere to a person or cause with strong affection.
webster_full: CLING, v.i. — 1. To adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast upon, especially by winding round or embracing; as, the tendril of a vine clings to its support; the infant clings to its mother. 2. To adhere closely with affection; to be devoted; to follow closely. Cleave to that which is good (Rom 12:9).
CLINGING, ppr. — Adhering closely; sticking to; holding fast.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 30:20
That thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days.
Psalm 63:8
My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.
Romans 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
1 Corinthians 6:17
But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
corruption_summary: Clinging to the LORD is corrupted by the diversified-loyalty register of late-modern faith—the soul that holds the LORD as one bond among many rather than as the supreme bond—and by the displacement clinging that fastens itself to His gifts (career, family, comfort, the affirming church) rather than to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Clinging in the biblical sense is exclusive: the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty. The diversified-loyalty register of contemporary faith corrupts this by treating the LORD as one of several bonds the believer maintains—alongside career, family, identity-group, political tribe, friends, hobbies—rather than as the supreme bond that orders all the rest. The result is a faith that does not cling but merely affiliates: present at services, present in profession, present in the categories of self-identification, but not bound to the LORD with the whole weight of the soul. The biblical verb is sharper. Ruth clave unto Naomi at real cost (her people, her gods, her future); the saints who cleave unto the LORD their God are alive every one of you this day; the verb is exclusive because the LORD is alone worthy of an exclusive bond. Diversified loyalty is not modesty about devotion; it is the soul’s refusal to be bound to its proper object.

The more subtle corruption is displacement clinging: the soul attaches itself, often unawares, to the gifts of the LORD rather than to the LORD Himself. The career becomes the bond; the spouse becomes the bond; the children become the bond; the comfortable house, the affirming church, the satisfying ministry, the political project become the bond. The gifts are good; the displacement is the corruption. When the gift is taken or threatened—the career lost, the spouse buried, the child wayward, the comfort stripped—the soul that clung to the gift discovers the substitution and is shaken to its foundations, because the foundation it had built upon was not the LORD but His provision. The recovery is the deliberate transfer of the clinging back to its proper object: thou art my portion, O LORD; whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever. The clinging that survives the loss of every gift is the clinging that was bound to the Giver.
roots_summary: Hebrew dābaq (to stick, cling, cleave) in its devotional uses (Deut 30:20; Ps 63:8); Greek kollaō (to join, glue, stick to) in Rom 12:9 and 1 Cor 6:17—the soul’s exclusive devotional adhesion to the LORD as supreme bond.
roots_lines: Hebrew dābaq (H1692) — to stick, cling, cleave; the great devotional-adhesion verb (Deut 4:4; 10:20; 11:22; 13:4; 30:20; Josh 22:5).
Greek kollaō (G2853) — to join, glue, stick to (Rom 12:9; 1 Cor 6:17; Acts 5:13; 17:34).
Greek proskollaō (G4347) — to join closely to (Matt 19:5; Mark 10:7; Eph 5:31).
Hebrew rādap ‘achar’ (H7291) — to follow hard after; cousin verb of the chasing pursuit that clinging produces.
usage: Biblical clinging is covenantal, exclusive, and total—the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty.
Displacement clinging fastens to the gifts rather than the Giver; the loss of the gift discovers the substitution and shakes the soul to its foundations.
My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me—the saint clings, and the upholding hand answers.

etymology: Latin exhortari, “to encourage strongly,” from ex- (intensive) + hortari (to urge). Renders the Greek parakaleō, “to call alongside, encourage, urge,” and protrepomai, “to turn forward, urge on.”
biblical_def: To exhort is the warm, urgent calling-alongside of one believer by another for the strengthening of faith, the stirring of love, the recovery from sin, and the perseverance unto the end. The Greek parakaleō is its principal verb—a verb the New Testament uses also of beseeching, comforting, and consoling, all of which are facets of the same near, personal, encouraging speech of one soul to another. Exhortation is therefore neither cold rebuke nor breezy chat; it is the sustained, hope-anchored, gospel-shaped pressing of truth upon a fellow saint with the affection of a brother and the urgency of one who knows the warning passages. Hebrews 3:13 sets its discipline at its highest pastoral pitch: but exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. Exhortation is the ordinary mutual ministry by which the saints keep one another soft to the Spirit’s touch; without it, sin’s deceitfulness hardens hearts unobserved. Paul’s epistles are saturated with the verb. He exhorts the Romans by the mercies of God; he exhorts the Corinthians to be reconciled to God; he exhorts the Thessalonians to abound more and more; he charges Timothy to preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. The exhorting gift is named among the gifts of the Spirit (he that exhorteth, on exhortation, Rom 12:8); the office of pastor includes it (holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers); and the ordinary believer is to practice it daily in the body. Exhortation differs from rebuke in tone (warmer), from comfort in direction (forward-pressing), from teaching in occasion (responsive to need), and from idle counsel in weight (anchored in the Word and the warning).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EXHORT as to incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct or course of action.
webster_full: EXHORT, v.t. — 1. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments to a good deed or to any laudable conduct or course of action. I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men (1 Tim 2:1). 2. To advise; to warn; to caution.
EXHORTATION, n. — The act of exhorting; the act of inciting to good deeds, with arguments or reasons; the form of words intended to incite and encourage.
scriptures: Hebrews 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
2 Timothy 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Romans 12:8
Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.
1 Thessalonians 4:1
Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
corruption_summary: Exhortation is corrupted by the therapeutic register that has dropped the warning passages and left only encouragement—and by the harsh register that knows how to rebuke but has lost the warm, calling-alongside affection that is exhortation’s biblical mark.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register of contemporary evangelicalism has emptied exhortation of its warning side. The believer is to be encouraged constantly, affirmed at every turn, comforted in distress, and built up in self-esteem—but never pressed with the hard, urgent, today-shaped warnings that Hebrews 3:13 makes central to mutual exhortation. The deceitfulness of sin is at work in every saint, the warning says, and exhortation is the daily mutual ministry by which the body keeps itself from being hardened. Drop the warning and the verb decays into mere encouragement; pastoral oversight loses its prophetic edge; the saints, no longer pressed with today, lest any of you be hardened, drift quietly into the calcification the verse aims to prevent. The recovery is to put the warning back inside the encouragement: a warm, calling-alongside, hope-anchored pressing that includes the sober word the soul needs precisely because the deceitfulness of sin is real.

The opposite corruption is the harsh register that has retained the warning and lost the warmth. The brother knows how to rebuke but has lost the calling-alongside affection that is exhortation’s biblical mark; correction is delivered without the consolation, the warning without the come-let-me-walk-with-you, the truth without the love that makes the truth bearable. Exhortation is by definition near, personal, and affectionate: the brother who exhorts another stands beside him as Paraclete-shaped speech does, not above him as judge. Recover both: warning and warmth, urgency and affection, the truth pressed home with the love that earns its hearing. The two together are what the New Testament means by exhortation—and the church saturated with that exhortation is the church kept soft to the Spirit’s touch and persevering to the end.
roots_summary: Greek parakaleō (to call alongside, encourage, urge) and protrepomai (to turn forward, urge on)—the warm, urgent, calling-alongside speech by which the saints keep one another soft to the Spirit’s touch.
roots_lines: Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside, exhort, encourage, comfort (the Paraclete verb).
Greek paraklēsis (G3874) — exhortation, encouragement, consolation (the noun).
Greek protrepomai (G4389) — to turn forward, urge on (Acts 18:27).
Greek noutheteō (G3560) — to admonish, warn (the sharper cousin verb of exhortation).
usage: Exhortation is warm and urgent at once—the calling-alongside affection of a brother combined with the gravity of one who knows the warning passages.
Exhort one another daily, while it is called To day—the ordinary mutual ministry by which the saints keep one another from the deceitfulness of sin.
Encouragement-only loses the warning; rebuke-only loses the warmth; biblical exhortation holds both, and the church is kept soft to the Spirit’s touch by it.

etymology: Latin exponere, “to set forth, explain,” from ex- (out) + ponere (to place). Renders the Greek diermeneuō, “to interpret thoroughly,” ektithemi, “to set forth,” and epiluō, “to loose, explain.”
biblical_def: To expound is to open up the meaning of a text of Scripture—to lay out what is there, to make plain what is folded, to set forth the sense, scope, and application of God’s Word for the understanding of the hearer. The supreme biblical model is the risen Christ on the Emmaus road: beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself; and later in the upper room, He opened... their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures. Exposition—the verbal noun of expound—is therefore Christ’s own method of teaching: He takes the texts, He sets forth what they mean, He shows how they point to Him, He applies them to the hearer. Philip on the desert road expounds Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian eunuch and preaches Jesus from the text. Apollos in Ephesus, having been instructed more perfectly in the way of God by Aquila and Priscilla, mightily convinces the Jews by the scriptures. Paul at Rome expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening. Exposition is therefore the central element of biblical teaching: not the speaker’s thoughts illustrated occasionally by Scripture, but Scripture itself opened up so that the divine sense of the text becomes the substance of what is delivered. Faithful exposition has marks. It is grounded in the text; it follows the text’s grammar, context, and flow; it traces the text’s connection to the whole counsel of God and especially to Christ; and it presses the text’s sense home to the conscience and life of the hearer. It rejects on one side the topical sermon that uses a verse as pretext for the preacher’s opinions, and on the other the dry exegetical lecture that hands the hearer information without the application Scripture is given to produce. To expound is to set the text forth in such a way that the hearer meets, in the preacher’s voice, the voice of God speaking from His own Word.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EXPOUND as to explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture, a law, a statute.
webster_full: EXPOUND, v.t. — 1. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture, a law, a statute. 2. To lay open; to examine carefully; as, to expound one’s self.
EXPOUNDING, ppr. — Explaining; laying open the meaning; interpreting.
scriptures: Luke 24:27
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Acts 8:35
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
Acts 28:23
...he expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.
Nehemiah 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Biblical exposition is corrupted by the topical sermon that uses a verse as a launching pad for the speaker’s opinions while the text itself is left unopened—and by the dry exegetical lecture that opens the text technically but never presses its sense home to the conscience of the hearer.
corruption_paragraphs: The most pervasive contemporary corruption of exposition is the topical sermon in which a verse is announced, briefly read, and then abandoned as the speaker moves to the actual content of his talk: cultural commentary, personal anecdote, motivational application, the speaker’s opinions on the issues of the week. The text is the pretext; the divine sense of the passage is never opened up; the hearer leaves having heard the speaker’s thoughts illustrated occasionally by Scripture rather than Scripture itself laid out and applied. Nehemiah 8:8 is the standing rebuke: so they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Read the text, give its sense, cause the people to understand—not deliver the speaker’s reflections garnished with Scripture, but expound the Word so that the hearer meets God in His own speech.

The opposite corruption is the dry exegetical lecture that opens the text technically—explains the Greek tense, traces the literary structure, surveys the scholarly options—but never presses the sense home to the conscience and life of the hearer. The information has been delivered; the application has not. Biblical exposition is more than analysis; it is the setting forth of the text’s sense for the hearer, with the application Scripture itself is given to produce. The risen Christ on the road to Emmaus did not merely catalogue the Old Testament texts about Himself; He expounded them so that the disciples’ hearts burned within them. Recover both ends: the substantive opening of the text (against the topical pretext) and the warm pressing of the text home (against the dry lecture), and exposition recovers its biblical shape—Christ’s own method of teaching, by which the people of God hear the voice of God in the Word of God.
roots_summary: Greek diermeneuō (to interpret thoroughly), ektithemi (to set forth), and epiluō (to loose, explain); Hebrew pārash (to make distinct, Neh 8:8)—the laying-open of the text’s sense so that the hearer meets God in His own speech.
roots_lines: Greek diermeneuō (G1329) — to interpret thoroughly, expound (Luke 24:27).
Greek ektithemi (G1620) — to set forth, expose, explain (Acts 11:4; 18:26; 28:23).
Greek epiluō (G1956) — to loose, solve, explain (Mark 4:34, “he expounded all things to his disciples”).
Hebrew pārash (H6567) — to make distinct, declare; Neh 8:8’s “gave the sense.”
usage: Exposition is Christ’s own method—the risen Lord on the Emmaus road expounded the Scriptures concerning Himself.
Read the text, give its sense, cause the people to understand—Nehemiah 8:8 is the standing rebuke to the topical-sermon corruption.
Dry exegetical lecture opens the text and leaves it cold; biblical exposition opens it and presses its sense home until the hearer’s heart burns.

etymology: Old English fæstan, “to abstain from food.” Renders the Hebrew tsūm, “to abstain from food,” and the Greek nēsteuō, “to abstain from food for religious reasons.”
biblical_def: To fast, in Scripture, is to abstain from food (and sometimes from drink and other ordinary goods) for a religious purpose—chiefly to humble oneself before God, to seek His face in earnest prayer, to mourn for sin, to wait on Him for guidance or deliverance, and to discipline the body that the soul may give itself more wholly to the LORD. The Bible records personal fasts (David fasted and prayed for his sick child; Daniel fasted three full weeks; Anna served God with fastings and prayers night and day), corporate fasts (the Day of Atonement; the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months in Zechariah; the fast called by Jehoshaphat when the great enemy came against Judah), and the supreme fast of the Lord Jesus, who fasted forty days and forty nights in the wilderness before His ministry began. Christ assumes the practice of fasting in His disciples (when ye fast, not if ye fast) and corrects its abuses without abolishing the discipline; He explicitly answers the question why His disciples did not fast during His earthly presence with the prophecy that the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days—that is, throughout the entire interval between His ascension and return. The apostolic church practiced fasting (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23); Paul ranks fastings among the marks of an apostolic ministry (2 Cor 6:5; 11:27); and the historic church has kept the discipline through every age. Isaiah 58 sets the most extended biblical theology of fasting at its sharpest: the fast God chooses is not mere abstinence with the spirit unchanged, but the fast that breaks every yoke, deals bread to the hungry, brings the poor into the house, and is matched by inward humbling and outward mercy. Fasting therefore is no work meriting reward; it is a posture, a deliberate emptying, by which the soul makes room for God where ordinary appetites have crowded Him out. Its primary register is humbling before God; its secondary effect, often surprising in its weight, is the recovery of spiritual hunger, the sharpening of prayer, and the loosening of the body’s tyrannical hold on the soul’s affections.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FAST as to abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time; in a religious sense, to abstain from food for the mortifying of the body, or as a token of grief, sorrow and affliction.
webster_full: FAST, v.i. — 1. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time; as, to fast a day or a week. 2. To abstain from food voluntarily, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, sorrow and affliction.
FAST, n. — Abstinence from food; properly, a total abstinence; voluntary forbearance of food, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, mourning, sorrow, or affliction.
scriptures: Matthew 6:16-18

Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast... But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret.
Isaiah 58:6-7

Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry...
Acts 13:2-3

As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Matthew 9:15

And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast.
corruption_summary: Fasting is corrupted, on one side, by the modern evangelical neglect that has quietly dropped the discipline as Old Covenant or merely Catholic, against Christ’s own when ye fast—and on the other by the dietary-and-wellness rebranding that fasts for body composition, autophagy, and clarity rather than for the humbling of the soul before God.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern evangelicalism has, in much of its practice, quietly dropped the discipline of fasting—often by treating it as an Old Covenant practice not binding under the New, or as a residual Catholic-and-Orthodox liturgical habit foreign to gospel freedom. Christ’s own teaching refuses both excuses. He says when ye fast, not if ye fast; He announces that the bridegroom’s absence will be precisely the era in which His disciples fast; the apostles fast in Acts; Paul lists fastings among the marks of his ministry; the historic church has kept the discipline through every age. The recovery is not legalism but simple obedience to the assumed-practice of the New Testament church: regular fasting, often privately, as the Father in secret directs and rewards.

The contemporary culture has, meanwhile, rediscovered fasting in another key: intermittent fasting for body composition, prolonged fasts for autophagy and mental clarity, calorie restriction for longevity. The bodily benefits are real; the rebranding is the corruption. Biblical fasting is not body-optimization with a verse attached; it is the humbling of the soul before God for prayer, mourning, seeking, and the recovery of spiritual hunger—an essentially religious act with bodily incidentals. The believer who fasts only for the metabolic benefits has dropped the discipline’s actual purpose; the believer who fasts biblically often discovers the metabolic benefits as a secondary gift while the primary one—a soul humbled and a prayer sharpened—is being granted by the Father who sees in secret.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsūm (to abstain from food) and Greek nēsteuō (to fast)—the humbling of the soul before God by deliberate abstinence, assumed-practice of Christ’s disciples (when ye fast) and of the apostolic church.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsūm (H6684) — to abstain from food, to fast.
Hebrew tsōm (H6685) — a fast, a fasting (the noun).
Greek nēsteuō (G3522) — to fast, abstain from food for religious reasons.
Greek nēsteia (G3521) — fasting (the noun); 2 Cor 6:5; 11:27.
usage: Christ said when ye fast, not if ye fast—the discipline is the assumed-practice of His disciples throughout the bridegroom’s absence.
The fast God chooses (Isa 58) is matched by inward humbling and outward mercy—abstinence without changed spirit is not biblical fasting.
Intermittent fasting for body composition is bodily; biblical fasting is the humbling of the soul before God, with metabolic benefits as secondary gifts.

etymology: Old English forberan, “to bear with, endure, restrain.” Renders the Greek anecheō, “to hold up, bear with,” and anechō, “to put up with”; and the Hebrew chādal, “to cease, refrain.”
biblical_def: To forbear is the patient bearing-with of another’s faults, slowness, weakness, or offence, without immediate response in kind—the steady refusal to retaliate, the disciplined choice not to press a grievance, the long-suffering disposition that gives space for the other’s repentance, growth, or simply for the inevitable friction of fallen people living in close proximity. The verb runs through the New Testament’s relational ethics. Paul commands the Ephesians, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; he commands the Colossians, forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. The pairing is significant: forbearance and forgiveness stand together, but they are distinct. Forbearance bears with the offence in the moment; forgiveness releases the debt after. Forbearance is the disposition the saint brings to the steady, low-grade abrasions of life-together—the brother’s irritating habit, the sister’s thoughtless word, the spouse’s slow growth in a particular grace, the elder’s decision the believer privately disagrees with—all the friction that is the unavoidable concomitant of fallen people loving one another in real time. Without forbearance, the church is a powder keg of small grievances ready to be lit by the next offence; with it, the church is a body whose members give each other room to be imperfect and to grow. The supreme model is God Himself, who has shown much longsuffering toward the vessels of wrath, and whose forbearance and longsuffering are reckoned by Paul as facets of His goodness leading sinners to repentance (Rom 2:4). The saint who has been borne with by such a God is to bear with others in the measure of what he has received.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FORBEAR as to keep away from; to abstain; to refrain; to spare; to treat with indulgence and patience; to bear with.
webster_full: FORBEAR, v.i. — 1. To keep away from; to abstain. 2. To pause; to delay. 3. To refrain; to be patient.

FORBEAR, v.t. — 1. To avoid voluntarily; to decline; to abstain from. 2. To treat with indulgence and patience; to bear with. Forbearing one another in love (Eph 4:2). 3. To spare; to withhold from action.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:2
With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love.
Colossians 3:13
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
Romans 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
2 Timothy 2:24
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient.
corruption_summary: Forbearance is corrupted by the modern reflexive register of immediate offence-taking and grievance-airing—every friction reported, every irritation aired, every slight pressed—and by the inverse error of treating forbearance as the toleration of unrepented sin or grave injury, which it never was.
corruption_paragraphs: The reflexive offence-taking of the contemporary register is the precise opposite of forbearance. Every friction is reported, every irritation is aired, every slight is pressed—often publicly, often immediately, often before the offender has the chance even to know what offence has been taken. The discipline of bearing with one another in love, of giving the other room to be imperfect, of not pressing every grievance, of overlooking what can be overlooked, has nearly vanished. The church absorbs the cultural register: brothers report each other to the elders for slight offences they could have borne with; spouses bring small grievances to the level of grave breaches; congregational life is fractured by accumulated little reckonings that forbearance would have absorbed at source. The recovery is the deliberate retraining of the soul to absorb the small abrasions, to overlook what can be overlooked, to extend the room the saint has himself received in such abundance from God.

The opposite and necessary qualification is that forbearance is not the toleration of unrepented sin or of grave injury. Scripture commands the discipline of Matthew 18 for sins that breach fellowship; it commands the public rebuke of false teaching; it commands the protection of the weak from real harm. Forbearance is the disposition for the steady, low-grade abrasions of life-together—not the discipline that handles grave offence, persistent unrepentance, or serious injury. The two must be held together: forbearance with the small things, formal process with the grave ones; longsuffering with the brother’s irritating habit, church discipline with the brother’s scandalous sin. Confuse the two and one of two corruptions follows: either the soul bears nothing and turns every friction into formal grievance, or the soul bears everything and tolerates what ought to have been confronted. The biblical discipline keeps the two distinct and applies each in its place.
roots_summary: Greek anecheō and anechō (to hold up, bear with, put up with); Hebrew chādal (to cease, refrain)—the patient bearing-with of another’s faults in the disposition Paul pairs with forgiveness in Eph 4 and Col 3.
roots_lines: Greek anecheō / anechō (G430) — to hold up, bear with, endure, put up with.
Greek anochē (G463) — forbearance, tolerance (Rom 2:4; 3:25).
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience (the cousin virtue paired with forbearance).
Hebrew chādal (H2308) — to cease, refrain (the negative-side restraining verb).
