Without forbearance, the church is a powder keg of small grievances; with it, the body gives its members room to be imperfect and to grow.
Forbearance is for the steady, low-grade abrasions of life-together; grave offence and unrepentant sin call for the formal process Scripture also commands.

etymology: Old English fullfyllan, “to fill up, complete,” from full + fyllan (to fill). Renders the Greek plēroō, “to fill up, complete, accomplish,” teleō, “to bring to an end,” and the Hebrew mālē’, “to fill, to fulfill.”
biblical_def: To fulfill is to bring to fullness or completion—to fill up what was begun, to accomplish what was promised, to complete what was prefigured. Two biblical uses dominate. First and supremely, Christ fulfills the law and the prophets: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil; all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me; that the scripture might be fulfilled is the constant refrain of the Gospels, especially Matthew and John. The Christological fulfillment is multi-layered: Christ keeps the moral law in His active obedience; He pays the law’s penalty in His passive obedience; He embodies the law’s typological prefigurations (the Passover Lamb, the True Israel, the Greater David, the Better Adam); He fulfills the prophets’ predictions in His person, work, and kingdom. The Old Testament is, in a profound sense, an unfulfilled text whose meaning becomes plain in the Christ who fulfills it. Second, the saint fulfills the law of Christ in his life: love is the fulfilling of the law; bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ; the believer fulfills the righteousness of the law not by works to earn standing but as the Spirit-wrought fruit of life in Christ. The Father fulfills His purposes through providence (the counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations); the Spirit fulfills His ministry in applying the redemption Christ accomplished; the church fulfills the Great Commission as she carries the gospel to the nations; the saint fulfills his ministry by completing what the Lord has given him to do (I have finished my course). And the final fulfillment is eschatological: the consummation when all things in heaven and earth shall be gathered together in one in Christ, the bringing of God’s purposes to their appointed end at the day of the Lord. To fulfill is therefore a verb that gathers up the whole story: promise made, promise kept; type prefigured, type embodied; law given, law completed; mission entrusted, mission accomplished; kingdom inaugurated, kingdom consummated—all in the Christ who is Himself the great Yea and Amen of every promise of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FULFIL as to accomplish; to perform; as a promise, prophecy, or threat; to bring to full execution; to complete; to satisfy the requirements or expectations of.
webster_full: FULFIL, v.t. — 1. To accomplish; to perform; as a promise, prophecy, or threat; to bring to full execution. Even so it must be that the scriptures should be fulfilled (Mark 14:49). 2. To complete; to bring to its end; as, to fulfil a course of years. 3. To accomplish what was intended; as, to fulfil one’s designs. 4. To answer in execution or event, as a prediction; as, to fulfil the prophecies. 5. To complete in obedience; as, to fulfil the law.
FULFILLING, ppr. — Accomplishing; performing; executing; answering in event.
scriptures: Matthew 5:17-18

Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
Luke 24:44

And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
Romans 13:10
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Fulfillment is corrupted, on one side, by dispensational and liberal-critical traditions that dehistoricize, postpone, or deny the Christological fulfillment of the Old Testament; and on the other by the antinomian register that hears fulfilled as abolished, missing Christ’s explicit denial that He came to destroy the law.
corruption_paragraphs: Two interpretive traditions corrupt the doctrine of fulfillment by misplacing the Christological center. Strict dispensationalism, at its hardest forms, postpones much of the Old Testament’s promised fulfillment to a future earthly Jewish kingdom and reads the apostolic claim that the Scriptures are fulfilled in Christ as referring chiefly to a parenthetical ‘church age’ rather than as the substantive fulfillment of the Old Testament itself. Liberal-critical reading goes the other direction, dehistoricizing the texts so thoroughly that the very notion of fulfilled predictive prophecy collapses into a literary motif. Both miss the New Testament’s plain claim: all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. The Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ—His person, His work, His kingdom—and that fulfillment is the unifying claim of apostolic exegesis from Luke 24 to Revelation 22.

The opposite corruption is the antinomian register that hears fulfilled as abolished. Christ explicitly denied this in the very breath He used the word: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. The law’s ceremonial prefigurations are fulfilled in Christ’s priestly work and so cease as types whose substance has come; the law’s civil arrangements were tied to Israel’s national situation and apply in their general equity; the law’s moral substance is the eternal righteousness of God, fulfilled by Christ on the believer’s behalf and fulfilled, by the Spirit, in the believer’s sanctified life—love is the fulfilling of the law. The verb fulfill therefore is not the cancellation of the Old Testament but its completion; not the displacement of the moral law but its embodiment in Christ and reproduction in His people. Both errors are corrected by the same biblical doctrine: the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ, and the moral law is fulfilled in the love that the Spirit produces in those united to Him.
roots_summary: Greek plēroō (to fill up, complete, accomplish) and teleō (to bring to an end); Hebrew mālē’ (to fill, to fulfill)—the great verb of promise kept, type embodied, law completed, and mission accomplished in the Christ who is Himself the Yea and Amen of every promise of God.
roots_lines: Greek plēroō (G4137) — to fill up, complete, accomplish, fulfill (the great Matthean fulfillment verb).
Greek teleō (G5055) — to bring to an end, complete, accomplish (‘it is finished’).
Hebrew mālē’ (H4390) — to fill, to fulfill, to accomplish.
Greek sumplēroō (G4845) — to fill up completely, fulfill (Luke 9:51, ‘when the time was come that he should be received up’).
usage: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil—Christ’s own denial that fulfillment is abolition.
The Old Testament is, in a profound sense, an unfulfilled text whose meaning becomes plain in the Christ who fulfills it.
Love is the fulfilling of the law—the moral substance of the law is fulfilled, by the Spirit, in the believer’s sanctified life.

etymology: Old English gaderian, “to gather, collect, assemble.” Renders the Hebrew qābats, “to gather, collect,” and ’āsaph, “to gather, take in”; and the Greek sunagō, “to lead together, gather,” and episunagō, “to gather together upon.”
biblical_def: Gather is one of Scripture’s great divine verbs: the action by which God draws His scattered people to Himself, the harvester gathers the wheat into the barn, the shepherd gathers the lambs in his arms, and the King at the end of the age gathers His elect from the four winds. The Old Testament repeats the gathering promise to a scattered Israel: I will gather you from the people, and assemble you out of the countries where ye have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel. Christ takes the verb on His own lips with deepest affection at the Lord’s lament over Jerusalem: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!—a verse that lays bare both the tender persistence of Christ’s gathering will and the awful reality of the gathered ones’ refusal. He continues the theme in His Olivet discourse: and he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Paul speaks of the gathering together unto him (2 Thess 2:1) as a name for the church’s consummation in Christ’s presence. Beyond these decisive uses, the verb governs ordinary church life: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them; not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; the apostles gather the multitudes to hear the Word; the church gathers on the Lord’s day for worship. There is also a gathering of judgment: the tares are gathered first and bound in bundles to be burned, the chaff is gathered and burned, the kings of the earth are gathered to the battle of the great day of God Almighty. The verb therefore has its two faces: the gracious gathering of the elect to Christ for life, and the judicial gathering of the rebel for wrath. Both are God’s acts; both are inevitable; and which gathering one is gathered into is settled by the response of the heart to the present gathering call of the gospel: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GATHER as to bring together; to collect; to assemble; to convene; to draw together from distant or remote places; to bring into one place or one body.
webster_full: GATHER, v.t. — 1. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things into one place, or into one aggregate body. 2. To collect, as fruits; to pluck and pick up. 3. To bring into one body or interest; to associate. 4. To collect in abundance; to accumulate; to amass. 5. To assemble; to congregate; to convene. 6. To gain by induction or inference.
GATHERING, ppr. — Collecting; assembling; bringing together; drawing together.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
Matthew 24:31
And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.
Hebrews 10:25
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
2 Thessalonians 2:1
Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him...
corruption_summary: The gathering of God’s people is corrupted by the consumer-spirituality register that treats the Lord’s Day gathering as an optional amenity and by the streaming-church habit that has displaced the actual assembling with a screen-mediated facsimile—against Christ’s own tender will to gather and Hebrews 10’s plain command not to forsake the assembling.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord’s Day gathering of God’s people is, in Scripture, a non-negotiable expression of the gathering Christ Himself accomplishes in His people—where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them; not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together. The consumer-spirituality register of contemporary evangelicalism has corrupted this by treating Sunday assembly as one option among many for the weekend—attended when convenient, skipped when inconvenient, chosen or abandoned by personal preference as one chooses a restaurant. The very tenderness of Christ’s lament over Jerusalem (how often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not) carries forward as the standing rebuke of every soul who refuses His present gathering call.

The streaming-church habit, born of necessity and now retained by preference, is a closely related corruption. The believer is ‘at church’ in front of a screen, watching a service from his couch, and counts himself gathered when Scripture knows nothing of the category. The gathering of the saints is by definition bodily co-presence: bodies in one place, voices in one room, bread broken among real hands, the laying-on of hands and the holy kiss and the looking each other in the eye—none of which a screen mediates. The streaming option has real and limited uses (the genuinely sick, the providentially hindered, the homebound saint) but it is not the gathering. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of the practice: the saint, like the saints of every age, gathered bodily with his local church on the Lord’s day, taking his ordinary place among the assembled people in whose midst Christ has promised to be.

etymology: Old French estriver, “to contend, struggle.” Renders the Greek agōnizomai, “to contend in the games, struggle, fight,” and athleō, “to compete as an athlete”; and the Hebrew rīb, “to contend, strive,” and lācham, “to fight.”
biblical_def: To strive, in the Christian life, is to contend with sustained, deliberate, athletic effort—in prayer, in the faith, against indwelling sin, for the souls of others, and to enter at the strait gate. The Greek agōnizomai carries the picture of the athlete in the games: every nerve engaged, every muscle taut, the long discipline of training meeting the climactic moment of competition. Christ Himself uses the verb at the strait gate: strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able. The contrast is sharp: seeking is what the many do and fail; striving is what the saved one does and enters. Paul takes the same verb and runs it across his ministry: he strives, according to his working, which worketh in me mightily; he charges the Corinthians, every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things; he commends Epaphras as always labouring fervently for you in prayers (the verb is agōnizomai); he describes his own ministry as a striving (Col 1:29). The Christian life is therefore, in one of its central images, an agonistic struggle: not the easy drift of cultural Christianity but the disciplined athletic exertion of those who have been called to run a race, fight a fight, and contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. Striving in Scripture has its proper objects: striving against sin (Heb 12:4 — ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin), striving in prayer for the saints, striving together for the faith of the gospel, striving to enter the kingdom. It is paired with the assurance that the striving is in the Spirit’s strength, not the flesh’s, and that the prize at the end is worth every nerve of the contest: an incorruptible crown, an unfading inheritance, the Master’s well done.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STRIVE as to struggle in opposition to another; to make efforts to overcome or surmount; to labor hard; to strain; to exert effort to obtain something, or to defend a cause.
webster_full: STRIVE, v.i. — 1. To make efforts; to use exertions; to endeavor with earnestness; to labor hard; applicable to exertions of body or mind. Strive to enter in at the strait gate (Luke 13:24). 2. To struggle in opposition to another; to be in contention; to oppose. 3. To vie; to contend in emulation; as, to strive to excel.
STRIVING, ppr. — Making efforts; struggling; contending; using exertions.
scriptures: Luke 13:24
Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.
1 Corinthians 9:24-25
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things...
Hebrews 12:4
Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.
Colossians 1:29
Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.
corruption_summary: Striving is corrupted by the easy-cultural-Christianity register that has dropped the athletic vocabulary of the New Testament for the gentler image of drifting along with the church program—and by the inverse corruption that strives in the flesh by sheer willpower rather than according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.
corruption_paragraphs: The athletic vocabulary of the New Testament has nearly disappeared from contemporary evangelical preaching. Sermons that summon hearers to strive to enter in at the strait gate, that warn that many will seek to enter in, and shall not be able, that press the picture of the runner straining for the prize and the soldier enduring hardness and the boxer beating his body to keep it under, are increasingly rare. In their place is the gentler image of drifting along with the church program: come on Sunday, give what you can, be encouraged, try to be a better person, do not be too hard on yourself. The biblical pattern is sharper. The Christian life is an agon, a contest, a striving; the saint is an athlete in training, a soldier in active service, a contender for a prize whose obtaining is at the end of a course that costs every nerve. Recover the apostolic register, and the church recovers the seriousness the New Testament uniformly assumes.

The opposite corruption is to strive in the flesh by sheer willpower—the moralist’s gritted-teeth attempt to win the contest by personal force, without reference to the Spirit’s strength on which the apostles always grounded their own striving. Paul says of his own striving: according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. The striving is real, sustained, and athletic; but it is the Spirit’s power that works in the saint, and the saint who tries to strive without that power either burns out or hardens into self-righteousness. Recover both ends: the real, athletic, costly striving the New Testament uniformly commands, and the grounding of that striving in the Spirit’s mighty working—not flesh-grit, but Spirit-strength applied through the disciplined exertions of the saint.
roots_summary: Greek agōnizomai (to contend in the games, struggle) and athleō (to compete as athlete); Hebrew rīb (to contend) and lācham (to fight)—the agonistic, athletic exertion of the Christian life, grounded in the Spirit’s mighty working.

The striving is real, but the strength is the Spirit’s: according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.

etymology: Old English growan, “to grow, increase, flourish.” Renders the Greek auxanō, “to grow, increase,” and the Hebrew gādal, “to grow great, become strong.”
biblical_def: Growth, in Scripture, is the appointed pattern of every living thing God has made and especially of the regenerate soul, whose life is a maturing in grace and in the knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ. Peter sets the keynote command: but grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ; Paul prays for the Colossians that they may be increasing in the knowledge of God; the Ephesian believers are to grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ; the newborn babes are to desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. Growth is therefore not optional Christianity; it is the ordinary mark of regenerate life, as much as the growth of a healthy child is the mark of natural life. The patterns of biblical growth are several. There is growth in grace (the increasing experience of God’s favor and the increasing operation of His Spirit). There is growth in knowledge (the increasing apprehension of the doctrines of the faith and the person and work of Christ). There is growth in holiness (the increasing mortification of indwelling sin and the increasing vivification of the new man). There is growth in love (the increasing capacity for both the love of God and the love of neighbor). There is growth in usefulness (the increasing service rendered to the body and the world). And there is growth in likeness to Christ—the great end of all the other growths—until the saint at last attains, in the resurrection, the full measure of conformity to His glorified image. Growth happens by the appointed means: the Word (sincere milk, then strong meat), the sacraments, prayer, the assembling of the saints, the discipline of obedience, the providences of God by which the saint is exercised, and the indwelling Spirit who applies all the means. Growth has its seasons: rapid early growth at conversion, the long steady growth of mid-life, the deepening growth of the latter years; and its setbacks: dry seasons, fall-back, the necessary pruning by the Husbandman that prepares for fresh fruitfulness. To be a Christian is to be a growing thing; the unchanged believer at fifty whose grace, knowledge, holiness, love, and usefulness are no greater than at conversion is the most serious pastoral concern Scripture knows.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GROW as to increase in size or stature, by a natural and insensible addition of matter, through nutrition; to enlarge; to extend; in scripture, to advance in moral or religious life; to make progress in grace.
webster_full: GROW, v.i. — 1. To increase in size or stature, by a natural and insensible addition of matter, through nutrition. 2. To be augmented in size by accretion or addition of matter. 3. To advance; to make progress; to improve. Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet 3:18). 4. To increase in degree; to be augmented; as, vegetables grow ripe; pride grows offensive.
GROWING, ppr. — Increasing in bulk or stature; advancing; making progress.

But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
Ephesians 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.
1 Peter 2:2
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.
Colossians 1:10
That ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God.
corruption_summary: Growth is corrupted by the static-conversion register that treats the new birth as the whole story and growth as an optional extra—and by the inverse register that frenetically pursues every new spiritual technique and program without the patient ordinary-means growth Scripture actually describes.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of contemporary evangelicalism treats conversion as the whole Christian story: the sinner’s prayer is prayed, the decision is registered, the new birth is announced, and the work is essentially complete; subsequent growth in grace is an optional extra for the unusually serious. Scripture knows nothing of this static Christianity. The new birth is the beginning; growth is the appointed pattern of the regenerate life; the unchanged believer at fifty whose grace, knowledge, holiness, love, and usefulness are no greater than at conversion is the most serious pastoral concern Scripture knows. The recovery is the recovery of growth as ordinary and expected: every believer is to be growing, every season is to leave its mark on the soul, every providence is to be the means of some increase, every Sunday a small step forward in grace and the knowledge of Christ.

The opposite corruption is the frenetic pursuit of every new spiritual technique, program, conference, retreat, breakthrough method, deliverance ministry, or charismatic intensification, on the assumption that ordinary growth is too slow and what the soul needs is a shortcut to maturity. Scripture provides no such shortcut. Growth is by appointed means—the Word, the sacraments, prayer, the assembled saints, the disciplines of obedience, and the providences of God—applied patiently across years. The newborn babe grows by milk and the mature by strong meat; the branch grows by abiding in the Vine; the tree planted by the rivers of water brings forth its fruit in its season. The cure for slow growth is not a new program; it is the patient, faithful, ordinary use of the means God has appointed, sustained over the long years that growth in Christ actually requires.
roots_summary: Greek auxanō (to grow, increase) and Hebrew gādal (to grow great)—the appointed pattern of the regenerate life by the ordinary means God has provided, across the long years that maturity in Christ actually requires.

Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ—Peter’s closing command states the whole pattern.
The cure for slow growth is not a new program; it is the patient, faithful, ordinary use of the appointed means across the long years maturity requires.

etymology: Old French garder, “to keep, watch over,” from a Germanic root meaning “to watch.” Renders the Greek phulassō, “to guard, keep, preserve,” and tēreō, “to watch over, keep”; and the Hebrew shāmar, “to keep, watch, preserve.”
biblical_def: To guard is to keep watch over with the active intent of protecting what is committed to one’s charge—the heart, the deposit of sound doctrine, the soul against the adversary, the flock against wolves, the church against false teaching. The verb in Scripture is therefore both inward and outward, personal and pastoral, defensive and watchful. Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life is the great inward charge of Proverbs—and the verb is nātsar, the close cousin of shāmar, both meaning to guard. The heart is the source from which life issues; it must be guarded as the city’s well-spring is guarded. Paul charges Timothy twice in his pastoral epistles: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings; and that good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us. The good deposit—the apostolic gospel, the sound doctrine, the rule of faith—is committed to each generation as a trust to be guarded, defended, transmitted intact. Peter announces that the saints are kept (guarded) by the power of God through faith unto salvation: the divine guarding of the elect by His power. Philippians 4:7 promises that the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep (guard) your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus—the same verb pictured as a garrison around the soul that has cast its care upon the Father. Guarding therefore has its three biblical horizons: God guards His saints; the saints guard their hearts; and the ministers and church guard the deposit of doctrine. Each guarding is necessary; none can be omitted; the church that loses any one of them weakens; the church that holds all three stands.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GUARD as to keep watch over, for protection or defense; to preserve from injury or attack; in religion, to keep, as a charge or trust.
webster_full: GUARD, v.t. — 1. To secure against injury, loss, or attack; to defend; to protect; to keep in safety. 2. To accompany, for protection; to escort. 3. To save the appearance, or maintain a respectful conduct; as, to guard one’s words. 4. In scripture, to keep, as a charge or trust; as, to guard the doctrine, to guard the heart.
GUARDING, ppr. — Defending; protecting; keeping in safety; watching over.
scriptures: Proverbs 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
1 Timothy 6:20
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.
2 Timothy 1:14
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
Philippians 4:7
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Guarding is corrupted by the unguarded-heart culture that lets every input reach the soul without filter—and by the unguarded-doctrine culture that holds the apostolic deposit so loosely that every novelty is welcomed, no boundary is held, and the trust committed to the present generation is leaked away without resistance.
corruption_paragraphs: The unguarded-heart culture is the inevitable product of a media environment in which every input reaches the soul without filter, every screen-scroll deposits a stream of images and ideas into the inner life, every notification interrupts what attention guarding the heart requires, and every algorithm shapes the affections by what it serves the eye. Proverbs’ charge to keep thy heart with all diligence presumes that the heart is keepable—that the saint chooses what is admitted to the gates of his soul, that the eye-gate and the ear-gate and the imagination-gate are real watchposts, and that what is allowed to enter shapes what issues out into life. Recover the inward discipline: deliberately filter inputs, deliberately disengage from sources that pollute, deliberately fill the heart with what is true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report—and the issues of life shift accordingly.

The unguarded-doctrine culture is the pastoral and ecclesial counterpart. The deposit of sound doctrine committed to Timothy and through him to every faithful minister and church is increasingly held with a light grip in the contemporary church: novelty is welcomed for novelty’s sake, the historic creeds and confessions are treated as period pieces rather than as the church’s collective discernment of the apostolic deposit, theological boundaries are felt as exclusionary rather than as the church’s protection, and the trust committed to the present generation is leaked away without resistance. Paul’s charge is sharper. Keep that which is committed to thy trust—guard it, defend it, transmit it intact. The faithful minister and the faithful church are stewards of a trust that does not belong to them and that they must hand on to those who come after them in the same condition in which they received it. Recover the doctrine of guarding, and the unguarded heart is re-fortified and the unguarded deposit is restored to its trustees—against the day when every steward shall give account.

etymology: Old English swerian, “to swear, take an oath.” Renders the Hebrew shāba, “to swear,” literally “to seven oneself” (oath-taking by sevens), and the Greek omnuō, “to swear, take an oath.”
biblical_def: To swear, in Scripture, is to take an oath—to invoke God’s name and witness in confirmation of one’s word, binding oneself under the most awful sanction to the truth of what is sworn or the performance of what is promised. Oath-taking is biblical: God Himself swears (by myself have I sworn, saith the LORD); He confirms His promise to Abraham with an oath (that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation); the patriarchs swear; the magistrates swear; witnesses swear in formal proceedings; and the New Testament shows the apostles using solemn oath-language (God is my witness; before God, I lie not). Christ’s teaching on swearing in the Sermon on the Mount—swear not at all... but let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay; for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil—has been read by some traditions (Anabaptist, Quaker) as a categorical prohibition of all oath-taking; the historic Reformed and Lutheran churches have read it as a prohibition of the casual, evasive, manipulative oath-swearing of the surrounding culture, not as the abolition of lawful and solemn oaths before magistrates and in formal civil and ecclesial life—a reading reinforced by Christ’s own answer under adjuration in Matthew 26 and the apostles’ solemn oath-language across the epistles. The biblical regulation of swearing is therefore threefold. What may be sworn: only what is true and what one will perform. By whom one may swear: only by God—not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, the temple, or one’s own head, all of which Christ explicitly forbids as substitutes for swearing by God Himself. And when one should swear: rarely, weightily, only when the matter calls for the solemn confirmation an oath supplies—and never in the casual, profane, or manipulative register of ordinary speech, where the third commandment’s severity is most often broken by those who imagine themselves religious.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SWEAR as to affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed; to make a solemn promise with an appeal to God for sincerity.
webster_full: SWEAR, v.i. — 1. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed. 2. To promise upon oath. 3. To give evidence on oath; as, to swear to the truth of a statement. 4. To use the name of God or any sacred thing in vain or profanely; as, to swear vainly, to swear profanely.
SWEAR, v.t. — 1. To utter, with an appeal to God or to some sacred object; as, to swear an oath. 2. To put to an oath; to cause to take an oath; as, to swear witnesses.
scriptures: Hebrews 6:13-14
For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself, Saying, Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee.
Hebrews 6:17-18

Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation...
Matthew 5:34-37
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne... But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
James 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
corruption_summary: Swearing is corrupted, on one side, by the casual profanity that drops God’s name and Christ’s name into ordinary speech as filler or expletive in plain violation of the third commandment—and on the other by the Anabaptist-style absolute prohibition that misreads Matthew 5 against the explicit biblical pattern of God’s own oaths and the apostles’ solemn oath-language.
corruption_paragraphs: The pervasive contemporary corruption of swearing is the casual profanity that has saturated ordinary speech: God’s name, Christ’s name, and the related sacred terms are dropped into ordinary speech as exclamation, filler, or expletive at a rate that earlier Christian centuries would have found shocking, and that the third commandment’s severity (the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain) plainly forbids. Believers absorb the surrounding register often unconsciously and bring it even into prayer and worship without recognizing the violation. Recover the third commandment’s gravity, and ordinary speech is purged of the profane uses that, more than any other corruption, demonstrate the shrunken doctrine of God in the contemporary church. The cleansing of speech is in this sense the most testable mark of a recovered fear of the LORD.

The opposite corruption is the Anabaptist-style absolute prohibition that reads Christ’s swear not at all as forbidding every oath in every circumstance, including solemn judicial oaths before magistrates and formal ecclesiastical oaths. The historic Reformed and Lutheran churches have rejected this reading on the explicit evidence of the biblical text: God Himself swears (Heb 6:13-18); Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and the prophets swear; Christ answers under formal adjuration in Matthew 26; Paul uses solemn oath-language repeatedly (Rom 1:9; 2 Cor 1:23; Gal 1:20; Phil 1:8; 1 Thess 2:5, 10). What Christ forbids in the Sermon on the Mount is the casual, evasive, manipulative oath-swearing of the surrounding culture—swearing by heaven or by the temple to escape the obligations of swearing by God, and the inflation of ordinary speech with oaths to compensate for habitual untruthfulness. The biblical regulation stands: only by God, only what is true, only when the matter genuinely calls for the solemn confirmation of an oath—and never in the casual or profane register that the contemporary corruption has normalized.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāba (to swear, literally “to seven oneself”) and Greek omnuō (to swear, take an oath)—the solemn invocation of God’s name in confirmation, regulated by the third commandment and Christ’s warnings against casual and evasive oaths.

Casual profanity that drops God’s name into ordinary speech as filler is the most pervasive contemporary violation of the third commandment’s severity.

etymology: Old English hatian, “to hate, treat as an enemy.” Renders the Hebrew sānē’, “to hate,” and the Greek miseō, “to hate,” used both negatively (the hatred of evil and the hatred Scripture forbids of one’s brother) and positively (the holy hatred of sin and the comparative hatred that prefers Christ above family and self).
biblical_def: Hate, in Scripture, has two opposite biblical uses and one biblical use that has long puzzled modern readers. The forbidden hate is the personal malice toward one’s brother that 1 John condemns as walking in darkness: he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because that darkness hath blinded his eyes; and again, whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him. This hate is the inward will-of-injury, the long-nursed bitterness, the settled enmity against another image-bearer; it is forbidden in every form, and its presence in the heart of one who claims to know God is a credible challenge to the claim. The commanded hate is the holy hatred of sin and the works of darkness, set by Scripture as the necessary correlate of the love of righteousness: ye that love the LORD, hate evil; I hate every false way; thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity (Ps 45:7, applied to Christ in Heb 1:9); the saint is to abhor that which is evil (Rom 12:9). Without holy hatred of sin, the love of righteousness atrophies into sentiment; with it, the love of righteousness has the moral seriousness Scripture assumes. The comparative hate is the one that has puzzled modern readers: if any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. The Hebrew idiom of comparative loving and hating (used in Gen 29:30-31 of Jacob loving Rachel and hating Leah—not personal malice, but preferring less) is here applied to the absolute priority of Christ: the disciple loves Christ so supremely that every other love—legitimate, deep, lifelong loves of family and self—is by comparison a hating. The same point is made plainly in Matthew 10:37: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. The verb hate therefore is freighted: forbidden in its personal-malice register, commanded in its holy-hatred-of-sin register, and applied comparatively in the demand for the supreme allegiance Christ requires of His disciples.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HATE as to dislike greatly; to have a great aversion to; opposed to love; in a more moderate sense, to dislike, to disapprove; in scripture, sometimes to love less.
webster_full: HATE, v.t. — 1. To dislike greatly; to have a great aversion to. It expresses less than abhor, detest, and abominate, unless pronounced with peculiar emphasis. 2. In scripture, to love less; to regard less than something else. If any man come to me, and hate not his father and mother... (Luke 14:26). The meaning is, to love less than Christ.
HATE, n. — Great dislike or aversion; hatred; detestation.
scriptures: Psalm 97:10
Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.
Romans 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
1 John 2:9
He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.
Luke 14:26
If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.
corruption_summary: Hate is corrupted in opposite directions by the present age: the therapeutic register treats all hatred as pathology, including the holy hatred of sin and evil Scripture commands—and the activist register weaponizes the word hate against any disagreement with the contemporary moral consensus, so that confessing biblical truth on contested matters is reflexively labeled hate speech.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register cannot recognize holy hatred. Scripture commands the saint to love what God loves and to hate what God hates—ye that love the LORD, hate evil; I hate every false way; abhor that which is evil—and the apostolic and prophetic literature is saturated with the holy hatred of sin, idolatry, and oppression that is the necessary correlate of the love of righteousness. The therapeutic culture has trained the believer to be uncomfortable with the very category. All hate is treated as pathology; all aversion as failure of love; all condemnation of evil as judgmentalism. The result is a Christianity that has lost the moral seriousness of its prophets and apostles, that can sing of love but cannot speak of hating what destroys the souls it loves, and that confuses the soft toleration of evil with the hard love of God for the people evil destroys. Recover the doctrine: love and holy hatred are inseparable; the love that does not hate what kills the beloved is not love but sentiment.

The opposite corruption is the activist register that weaponizes the word hate against any disagreement with the present moral consensus, so that confessing biblical truth on contested matters (abortion, sexual ethics, the exclusivity of Christ) is reflexively labeled hate speech and the speaker treated as a hater rather than as a witness. The biblical distinctions disappear: the holy hatred of sin (commanded) is conflated with personal malice toward sinners (forbidden), and the comparative love of Christ above all (Luke 14:26) is conflated with bigotry against those one is comparatively loving less. Recover the distinctions Scripture itself makes, and the believer regains both his liberty and his courage: he loves the image-bearer warmly even while he hates the sin that destroys him; he loves Christ supremely without ceasing to love family and self in their proper place; he refuses both the therapeutic collapse that calls holy hatred pathological and the activist collapse that calls biblical confession hate.

etymology: Old Norse kynda, “to light a fire.” Renders the Hebrew chārāh, “to burn, be hot,” bā‘ar, “to burn,” and qādach, “to kindle”; and the Greek anaptō, “to kindle,” and anazōpureō, “to stir into flame.”
biblical_def: To kindle in Scripture is to start, stir, or rouse a fire—literal in the lampstands of the tabernacle and the sacrificial flames upon the altar, figurative in the four great biblical fires of wrath, zeal, love, and the Spirit’s gift. The wrath of the LORD is kindled when His people break the covenant: and the LORD’s anger was kindled against Israel recurs across the historical books; kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. The zeal of the saints is kindled by the Word and the providences of God: David’s heart was hot within him, and while he was musing the fire burned. The love of God in the soul, dimmed by sin or coldness, is kindled afresh in seasons of recovery: I will betroth thee unto me for ever. And the gift of God in the minister is to be deliberately stirred into flame: Paul charges Timothy, I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up (kindle, anazōpureō) the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands—a participle picturing the live-coal of God’s grace that may sink to ash if not stirred but that bursts back into flame when the deliberate breath of prayer, Word, and use is applied. The kindling of fire is therefore a recurring biblical category for the action by which what was dormant is roused, what was cold is warmed, what was sinking is restored to flame. Pastoral application is direct. The cold heart is to be kindled by deliberate use of the means God has given to kindle it—the Word read with the prayer that God would set its truth on fire in the soul, the meditation that holds the truth long enough for the flame to catch, the prayer that calls upon the Spirit who is Himself a fire, the assembling of the saints around the kindled fires of others. The wrath of the LORD is averted by repentance; the zeal of the saint is stirred by the Word; the love of God is rekindled by recovering the cross; the gift of God in the minister is stirred up by the daily use of it. Each is at root a kindling.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KINDLE as to set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; figuratively, to inflame, as the passions; to exasperate; to rouse; to provoke; to excite to action.
webster_full: KINDLE, v.t. — 1. To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; as, to kindle a fire. 2. To inflame, as the passions; to exasperate; to rouse; to provoke; to excite to action; to heat; to fire; to animate; to incite; as, to kindle anger or wrath; to kindle resentment; to kindle the flame of love.
KINDLING, ppr. — Setting on fire; lighting; inflaming; rousing into action.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 1:6
Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.
Psalm 39:3
My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue...
Psalm 2:12
Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
Luke 12:49
I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?
corruption_summary: Kindling is corrupted by the cold-and-content register of the present church that has accepted the dimmed lamp as ordinary and has lost the discipline of deliberately stirring into flame the gift of God in the minister, the zeal of the saint, and the love of the redeemed for the Christ who came to send fire on the earth.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary church is widely cold and widely content to be so. The pastor whose gift has dimmed accepts the dimming as the maturing of his ministry; the saint whose love has cooled accepts the cooling as the inevitable settling of conversion’s early ardor; the congregation whose zeal has waned accepts the waning as the proper sobriety of the long Christian walk. Paul’s charge to Timothy refuses this. Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands: the verb pictures the live-coal that has sunk to ash and must be deliberately blown back into flame, not the resigned acceptance of a fire too weak to warm. The recovery is the discipline of deliberate stirring: the Word read with prayer that God set its truth on fire in the soul, the sustained meditation that holds the truth long enough for the flame to catch, the prayer that calls upon the Spirit who is Himself a fire, the assembling of the saints around the kindled fires of others.

Christ’s own word puts the standard at its sharpest: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? The Christ who came to send fire does not commission a cold church. The kindling is His, the means are His, but the discipline of stirring is the saint’s and the minister’s and the church’s. Where the kindling has been neglected, the recovery is deliberate: identify the sunk coal, name what would stir it (a season of fasting, a return to the cross-centered preaching, a recovery of the prayer meeting, an honest confession of dryness with brothers who will pray), and apply the breath. Where the kindling is fresh, the discipline is to keep it stirred: not to let the day’s busyness or the year’s comforts let the flame sink again. The fire Christ kindles is meant to burn through the whole of the saint’s life and the whole of the church’s history—and it does, where it is stirred.
roots_summary: Hebrew chārāh (to burn, be hot), bā‘ar (to burn), and qādach (to kindle); Greek anaptō (to kindle) and anazōpureō (to stir into flame, 2 Tim 1:6)—the rousing of dormant fire: wrath, zeal, love, and the gift of God.

Hebrew bā‘ar (H1197) — to burn, kindle.

Four biblical fires are kindled: the LORD’s wrath against sin, the saint’s zeal under the Word, the love of God in the soul, and the gift of God in the minister—each requires its own stirring.

etymology: Latin laborare, “to work, toil.” Renders the Greek kopiaō, “to grow weary by toil, labor to weariness,” and ergāzomai, “to work”; and the Hebrew ‘āmal, “to labor, toil,” and yāga, “to be weary, work hard.”
biblical_def: To labor, in Scripture’s ministerial and spiritual register, is the wearying, sustained, costly work of the saint and the minister in the things of God: the labor of preaching, of prayer, of pastoral care, of the daily mortification of sin, of bearing burdens in the body of Christ, and of the manual labor by which the believer eats his own bread and gives to him that needeth. The Greek kopiaō is the most freighted of the verbs: it does not simply mean to work; it means to work to weariness, to labor until tired. Paul saturates his ministry-language with it: therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God; I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me; let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine; greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us; my beloved brother and labourer with me in the gospel; and the great closing verse of 1 Corinthians 15: therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Christ Himself uses the verb pastorally in His invitation: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; and in His sending: the harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest. The biblical labour is therefore weighty work, deliberately undertaken, sustained over time, often to the point of exhaustion, and grounded in the assurance that in the Lord it is not in vain. The contrast in Scripture is sharp: labor in the Lord versus labor in the flesh (the latter being the wearying striving that achieves nothing because not grounded in grace); labor in the Lord versus idleness (the avoidance of labor that Paul roundly condemns in 2 Thess 3); and labor in the Lord versus the world’s labor for what perisheth (against which Christ commands, labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LABOR as exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained, as in agriculture and manufactures; toil; work; pains.
webster_full: LABOR, v.i. — 1. To exert muscular strength; to act or move with painful effort, particularly in service to another, or in any employment for hire. 2. To exert mental powers, in the performance of any business; to study; to take pains. 3. To toil; to be burdened. 4. To be in distress; to be pressed; to suffer.
LABOR, v.t. — To work at; to till; to cultivate. The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits (2 Tim 2:6).

Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Matthew 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
1 Timothy 5:17

corruption_summary: Christian labor is corrupted, on one side, by the comfort-and-balance register of contemporary middle-class faith that recoils from any labor sustained to weariness, treating exhaustion in the Lord’s work as poor self-care—and on the other by the flesh-driven workaholism that labors much but not in the Lord, and so is exhausted but not fruitful.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary register of comfort and balance recoils from the New Testament’s constant language of labor to weariness. Paul saying he laboured more abundantly than they all; Epaphras always labouring fervently for you in prayers; the elders to be honored especially for laboring in the word and doctrine; Mary who bestowed much labour on us; the apostle’s closing charge to abound in the work of the Lord because your labour is not in vain in the Lord—all of this sits uncomfortably with a Christianity that has absorbed the broader culture’s suspicion of any exhaustion in service. Exhaustion is reflexively treated as a failure of self-care; sustained labor in the Lord’s work is recast as unhealthy boundaries; the apostolic register is, in practice, set aside. Scripture is sharper. The Christian life is, in a real sense, a life of labor—labor to weariness, labor that costs, labor sustained over years. The grace that grounds it makes the labor possible and joyful, but does not eliminate the labor itself.

The opposite corruption is the flesh-driven workaholism that labors much without laboring in the Lord. Activity replaces dependence; energy replaces grace; the minister or saint runs hard but in his own strength, and the result is exhaustion without proportionate fruit, and often a slow embittering as the labor goes unacknowledged and the strength fails. Paul’s own qualification is essential: I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. The two clauses must stand together. Recover both ends. Refuse the comfort-and-balance retreat from sustained labor in the Lord, and refuse the flesh-driven labor that is not grounded in grace. The biblical pattern is sustained, costly, weariness-touching labor done in the Lord by the grace of God—and Scripture’s assurance to those who labor in that pattern is firm: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
roots_summary: Greek kopiaō (to grow weary by toil) and ergāzomai (to work); Hebrew ‘āmal (to labor) and yāga (to be weary, work hard)—the wearying, sustained, costly work of saint and minister, grounded in grace and never in vain in the Lord.

Hebrew ‘āmal (H6001) — to labor, toil; the noun ‘āmāl means “labor, trouble.”
